name: Scottish Gaelic
variety: Lewis Gaelic (Outer Hebrides), the variety of the JIPA illustration (Nance & Ó Maolalaigh 2021); differences in other Hebridean and mainland dialects are noted
sources: Nance, Claire; Ó Maolalaigh, Roibeard (2021). Scottish Gaelic. Journal of the International Phonetic Association 51(2): 261-275.
Ladefoged, Peter; Ladefoged, Jenny; Turk, Alice; Hind, Kevin; Skilton, St. John (1998). Phonetic structures of Scottish Gaelic. Journal of the International Phonetic Association 28: 1-41.
Nance, Claire; Stuart-Smith, Jane (2013). Pre-aspiration and post-aspiration in Scottish Gaelic stop consonants. Journal of the International Phonetic Association 43(2): 129-152.
Nance, Claire (2024). Scottish Gaelic. In Fox, Sue (ed.), Language in Britain and Ireland (3rd ed.). Cambridge University Press, 288-313.
Borgstrøm, Carl Hj. (1940). The Dialects of the Outer Hebrides. Norsk Tidsskrift for Sprogvidenskap, supplementary volume 1. Oslo.
Oftedal, Magne (1956). The Gaelic of Leurbost, Isle of Lewis. Norsk Tidsskrift for Sprogvidenskap, supplementary volume 4. Oslo.
Ternes, Elmar (2006). The Phonemic Analysis of Scottish Gaelic (3rd ed.). Dublin Institute for Advanced Studies.
Gillies, William (2009). Scottish Gaelic. In Ball, Martin J. & Müller, Nicole (eds.), The Celtic Languages (2nd ed.). Routledge.
contrasts: two series of voiceless stops: unaspirated (written b d g) and aspirated (written p t c); there are no voiced stops
after a stressed vowel the aspirated stops are preaspirated, so the contrast there is preaspirated against plain
broad against slender consonants: the slender partners of the dental stops are postalveolar affricates, of the velars palatal stops, of /s/ is /ʃ/, of /x/ is /ç/, of /ɣ/ is /j/
three-way contrasts in laterals and in coronal nasals: velarised dental, plain alveolar, palatalised dental
vowel length, nine vowel qualities including back unrounded /ɯ ɤ/, and ten diphthongs
nasal vowels, with a small functional load
in Lewis, a word accent that separates monosyllables from words of two or more syllables
allophony: preaspiration differs by dialect: in Lewis a stretch of breathy voice followed by voiceless [h]; in dialects such as Barra closer to [x], above all before velar stops
preaspiration is longest before velar and palatal stops and shortest before bilabials, and shorter after long vowels than after short ones
the stops written b, d, g have little or no voicing even between vowels
/u/ is central [ʉ] except next to velarised sonorants, where it is back; /a/ is retracted next to velarised sonorants; /ɯ ɤ/ are central or even front in Lewis
slender /ɾʲ/ is often a dental fricative [ð] in Lewis; the plain rhotic is a tap or approximant, trills are rare today
rt, rd and rs are retroflex in Lewis; most other dialects put [ʃ] or [ʂ] between r and t

an unwritten vowel, a copy of the preceding one, breaks up clusters of a sonorant and a following consonant made at a different place, after a short stressed vowel (Alba, gorm, ainm, falbh); it is as prominent as the vowel it copies
hiatus words (leabhar, latha, bogha) have two vowels in a row with no consonant; outside Lewis a glide, creak or glottal stop separates them
short vowels before the old tense sonorants ll, nn, m are diphthongs or long when the sonorant ends the word or stands before a consonant (ceann, donn, trom, cam, call)
/n/ is velar or palatal before velar and palatal stops
cn, gn are pronounced with [ɾ] and a nasal vowel (cnoc)
phonotactics: word-medial consonants are reported to close the preceding syllable rather than open the next (aran as ar.an)
long vowels stand mainly in the stressed first syllable
lenition is the only mutation shown in the spelling; nasalisation of initials after an, am, nan is not written and not used by all speakers
the consonants of a cluster agree in broad or slender quality

stress.rule: Stress falls on the first syllable of nearly all words; exceptions are some loanwords, compounds and adverbs (buntàta, an-diugh, Didòmhnaich).
stress.cues: pitch (in Lewis the word accent), duration and full vowel quality; unstressed vowels are short and mostly [ə], [ɪ] or [a]

rhythm.vowel_reduction: strong: unstressed vowels are short and reduced to a small set, mostly [ə], [ɪ] and [a]

length.notes: Long vowels are written with a grave accent and are slightly more peripheral than short ones. Preaspiration before an aspirated stop after a stressed vowel lasts on average 58 ms before bilabials, 83 ms before coronals and 80 ms before velars in Lewis (breathy and voiceless parts together; the voiceless part alone is 16, 32 and 34 ms), and is shorter after long vowels (Nance & Stuart-Smith 2013).

intonation.declarative: fall in pitch at the end of the phrase
intonation.yes_no_question: questions are marked by verbal particles (an, am, nach); a rising pitch has been described for Lewis
intonation.wh_question: not described in the sources consulted
intonation.continuation: not described in the sources consulted
intonation.accent_shape: in Lewis set by the word accent: low or rising on a monosyllable, high and falling from the first syllable of a longer word
intonation.notes: If the last syllable of a statement has the rising word accent, the rise is much reduced (Borgstrøm 1940, reported by Nance & Ó Maolalaigh 2021).

inventory.name: accent 1 (monosyllables, including words with an inserted copy vowel such as falbh, ainm)
accent 2 (words of two or more syllables, including hiatus words such as leabhar, bogha)
inventory.description: level high, falling or rising-falling pitch beginning on the stressed syllable

sandhi: the accent follows from the number of syllables: a word with an inserted copy vowel counts as one syllable, a hiatus word as two
tone.neutral_tone: unstressed words and syllables carry no accent of their own
tone.notes: The word accent is found in Lewis and in some north-west mainland dialects (Applecross), not in the southern Hebrides or most mainland dialects. The Chao numerals are schematic. eSpeak NG has no tone phonemes for this language.

phonation: preaspirated voiceless stops after stressed vowels, with breathy voice at the end of the vowel
aspirated voiceless stops at the beginning of words
ingressive speech on discourse markers and phrase-final words

problems: preaspiration is dropped after long vowels (bàta has none); the literature finds it shorter there, not absent
the kind of preaspiration is mixed: [h] before p and t but [x] or [ç] before c (mac as [maxk]), as in dialects such as Barra, while Lewis has [h] throughout and slender r as [ð] is a Lewis feature
there are no nasal vowels, also not after cn, gn (cnoc)
no word accent and no mark of hiatus
the velarised dental nasal uses the plain [n] (phoneme n[ is marked temporary), so the three nasals are not fully kept apart
several vowel rules are marked uncertain in gd_rules (è, ò, oi, ia, ua); leat comes out with [ɛ] instead of [a]
the voice is marked 'status testing'; the rule file is based on a description of the spelling, not on one dialect
IPA output prints the unaspirated stops as [b d ɡ] and most aspirated stops as plain [p t k]
good: preaspiration exists as a rule-driven phoneme with variants by the place of the stop (mac, cat, poca, aca, mic)
the inserted copy vowel (Alba, gorm, dearg, falbh)
two voiceless stop series: the unaspirated one is taken from the Icelandic table
diphthongs before ll, nn, m (ceann, donn, trom, cam, call)
velarised l, palatal [ʎ] and [ɲ], slender r as [ð], chd as [xk]
back unrounded vowels for ao and related spellings
initial stress and reduction of unstressed vowels

notes: Vowel formants are left out: the JIPA illustration gives them only as a plot in Bark, and the tables of Ladefoged et al. (1998) could not be checked.
